title: The one thing to watch instead of someone's promises
format: Talking head + a fast montage of your hands (Formats 46 @yemshaven montage + voiceover, Formats 48 @yemshaven crisp clips with rounded corners) + serif captions on black boxes (Formats 67 @philosophyminis, C4). Top title T2: plain white, no box, soft shadow, 'The one thing to watch instead of someone's promises' (your quote 'Trust your hands, not your mouth' goes on the black card at the end). One black phrase card for the quote at the end.
length: about 58 s (152 spoken words at about 2.6 a second); about 5-8 s more with your [gap] line.
hook: If I tell you I'm going to buy you a house and a car tomorrow morning, would you believe me?

record.where: Hallway (a plain stretch of wall), then 6-8 extra clips around the apartment for the montage.
record.how: Phone upright (9:16) at chest height. Start a step back and walk two slow steps towards the camera on the first line (like @jade_beason), then stand still and talk. Calm, sure, a little amused at the house-and-car line. Then film 6-8 clips of 2-3 seconds of ONLY your hands doing ordinary things: stirring a pot, typing, writing in a notebook, folding a shirt, washing a cup, tying your shoes.
record.props: Nothing in your hands for the talking part. For the montage, whatever is around (pot, notebook, laptop, laundry).

script:
If I tell you I'm going to buy you a house and a car tomorrow morning, would you believe me? Those are my words. But I probably wouldn't.

Words are so sweet, and they come naturally to us.

I started to pay more attention to my words in comparison with my actions. Because at the end of the day, it's not about what I say I'm going to do. It's about what I actually do. It's just about doing what you say you would do, being who you claim to be.

*[on screen: a quick montage of your hands doing things (cooking, typing, writing in a notebook, folding laundry), 2 cuts a second, while you keep talking]*

Saying it doesn't cost us much. Doing it costs us time and effort. And if something doesn't cost you much, it can't be evidence of much.

If someone says they're going to do something and they do something else, you don't trust what they said. You trust what they did.

*[on screen: black card, your accent serif, "Trust your hands, not your mouth."]*

Someone said it like this. Trust your hands, not your mouth.

[gap: optional, one closing line in your words, only if it's true for you (e.g. a promise you made yourself this year and whether your hands kept it). Or simply end on the quote.]

title: "Connected, no internet": what it means
format: Talking head with the explainer graphics beside you on half the screen, one running example (your home as a house on a street), built up step by step like @kodekloud (Formats 6, you liked its motion) + the TV/slide-beside-you feel of @nandini_mpe (Formats 64). Top title T3: white rounded box, black heavy sans, 'Connected, no internet?'. Captions C1: heavy caps, one word in an accent colour.
length: about 58 s (152 spoken words at about 2.6 a second).
hook: When your phone says "connected, no internet", it's telling you where the problem is.

record.where: Living room, next to wherever your Wi-Fi router or MiFi sits (a shelf or the TV stand).
record.how: Phone upright (9:16), you standing on the RIGHT half of the frame so the left half is free for the diagram. Hold your phone up to the camera on the first line (screen towards the lens, Wi-Fi settings open), then lower it. Point at the router when you say "the router". Clear, friendly teacher energy, medium pace.
record.props: Your phone with the Wi-Fi settings open; the router or MiFi in shot.

script:
When your phone says "connected, no internet", it's telling you where the problem is.

*[on screen: a phone Wi-Fi screen with "Connected, no internet" under the network name (generic, not your real network)]*

Think of your home as a house. Wi-Fi is the hallway inside it. It connects your phone and your laptop to the router.

The router is the receptionist. It passes messages in and out for every device in the house.

The modem is the front gate, where the line from outside comes in. And your internet provider, the company you pay, owns the road from your gate to the rest of the internet.

*[on screen: flat diagram building up beside you: phone → hallway (Wi-Fi) → receptionist (router) → gate (modem) → road (your provider) → the internet. A MiFi drawn as router + modem in one small box.]*

So "connected, no internet" means your phone reached the receptionist. The problem is further out, at the gate, the line, or your provider.

If every device in the house has lost internet, restart the router and the modem. If it's only your phone, look at your phone.

And on hotel or school Wi-Fi, it often means you haven't signed in on their login page yet.
changes:
- Topic from your kit 49 (Networking basics), segment 3 "Wi-Fi vs internet" and its Short 2 "Connected, no internet". The kit is an AI draft, so the wording was shortened to sound spoken.
- Kept the kit's house analogy (hallway, receptionist, front gate, road). The MiFi line moved into the diagram to keep the short under 60 s.
- Added the hotel / school login-page case (a common cause on public Wi-Fi).
- No personal story in it, so no [gap].
ournote:
1. Do you have a router or a MiFi at home you can show? If not, film next to the TV and we draw the router in the graphic.
2. Is your phone an iPhone or Android? Android says "Connected, no internet"; an iPhone shows "No internet connection" under the network name. We show whichever you use, or both.
3. This short can lead to the full Networking basics video (kit 49) when you record it.

title: Instagram will now guess your age with AI
format: Talking head + receipts: the article itself is the heading, a white card in the top third with the key line highlighted (@nandini_mpe, Formats 66) + a white rounded title box with black heavy sans for the topic (@funmiyakubu, Formats 69, T3) + caps captions with one coloured word (Formats 42, C1). hook: Instagram will now use AI to guess if you're a teenager, even if you put an adult birthday when you signed up, and move you into a stricter teen account.

record.where: Bedroom, sitting on the edge of the bed, window light from the side.
record.how: Phone upright (9:16), you in the lower two-thirds so the article card fits above your head. Newsy and curious, medium pace; slow down on "what the announcement doesn't say". Hold your phone with Instagram open in the first second, then put it on your lap.
record.props: Your phone with the Instagram app open (any feed, no private messages visible).

script:
Instagram will now use AI to guess if you're a teenager, even if you put an adult birthday when you signed up, and move you into a stricter teen account.

*[on screen: Meta's newsroom post "Expanding Teen Account Protections to Teens Around the World", 9 November 2026, as a card in the top third, the line about adult birthdays highlighted]*

Meta, the company that owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, announced it on the 9th of November. It's now going worldwide, so that includes Nigeria.

If the AI thinks you're a teenager, your account becomes a Teen Account. It goes private, only people you're already connected to can message you, and Meta limits what you see and your time on the app.

What I find interesting is what the announcement doesn't say. It doesn't say what the AI looks at to decide. And it doesn't say what an adult should do if it gets them wrong.

[gap: your reaction in one or two sentences, as you'd say it. For example, whether you think an app guessing your age from how you use it is fair, and why.]

Should an app be allowed to guess your age from how you use it?

- Your opinion is left as a [gap]: we did not write a view for you.
ournote:
1. Post this soon: the announcement is from 9 November 2026, so it is fresh this week and next.
2. What is your take (the [gap])? As an HCI student you could say whether guessing age from behaviour is fair, or what a good way to fix a wrong guess would look like.
3. Facts are only what Meta's post and the news reports say. Meta did not say how many accounts are affected or what signals the AI uses, so the script says that plainly and makes no guesses.

title: Study in Estonia with your spouse? The 2-year rule
format: Talking head + the official document as a receipt: a white card in the top third with the line highlighted yellow (@nandini_mpe, Formats 42) + a yellow box title (#FFE125, black bold sans) that types on in the first 1.5 s (Formats 42, T4) + two big number cards ("2 years", "€70 a day") cut in full-screen on flat colour (@aishahwasim, Formats 32). Captions C1. Cover line in search words: "Study in Estonia with spouse" + Nigerian flag.
length: about 56 s (146 spoken words at about 2.6 a second).
hook: Can you bring your husband or wife with you when you come to study in Estonia? Not straight away.

record.where: Kitchen, standing at the counter, a mug in your hand.
record.how: Phone upright (9:16), you in the lower two-thirds so the document card fits above you. Helpful big-sister energy, clear and calm; a small pause after "Not straight away." Say the numbers slowly (two years, 70 euros, 2,100 euros).
record.props: A mug (like the reference). No real documents or your own permit card on camera.

script:
Can you bring your husband or wife with you when you come to study in Estonia? Not straight away.

*[on screen: the Police and Border Guard Board's 2025 guide for students, slide "Inviting family member (spouse)", the two-year line highlighted]*

This is from the Police and Border Guard Board, the office that gives out residence permits here. Their 2025 guide for students says you have to live in Estonia on a residence permit for at least two years before you can invite your spouse.

A lot of master's programmes here are two years, so that's basically your whole programme.

*[on screen: "2 years", big]*

And your spouse can't get the long-stay visa on the same terms as a student. They have to show at least 70 euros for every day of the visa. That's about 2,100 euros a month.

*[on screen: "€70 a day ≈ €2,100 a month", big]*

So if you're married, plan for this before you apply. And don't just take an agent's word for it. You can email the Police and Border Guard Board's migration advisers your exact situation.

*[on screen: migrationadvice@politsei.ee]*
changes:
- New script, written in your voice from the official source below. No words of yours were changed.
- It does not say you are married or have family here.
ournote:
1. Facts come from the Police and Border Guard Board's own slides ("Students residing and working in Estonia", migration adviser Viktoria Petrova, 25.08.2025), shared by TalTech. One third-party site says something stricter, so if you want to be extra safe, email migrationadvice@politsei.ee before you post and ask whether the 2-year rule still applies in 2026 and whether PhD students are treated differently.
2. Search check (YouTube suggestions, 2026-11-16): people type "study in estonia with spouse", "estonia student visa with spouse" and "study in europe with spouse". That's why the title says it in those words.
3. If you know someone in Estonia who planned around this rule (and they're happy for you to mention it), one line about it after "your whole programme" would make it stronger. Leave it out otherwise.
4. A good follow-up short from the same official guide: you can stay in Estonia 270 days after your study permit ends (but it's already in your "What I wish I knew" kit, so only if you want a standalone one).
